name: SELFORGE
line: An iPhone alarm that keeps ringing until the camera has counted my pushups.
summary: SELFORGE is an iPhone alarm I can't swipe off: the siren runs until every mission on the alarm is done, whether that is pushups or squats counted by the camera, a QR code I have to walk to, or real outdoor daylight. It also tracks habits on home-screen widgets, and its Brick Mode blocks distracting apps until I've done my reps. Its mascot, Ember, is a flame drawn entirely in code.
why: A normal alarm can be silenced half asleep with one swipe. I wanted an alarm clock that "doesn't go off until it recognizes that I do a certain amount of pushups," with the count set per alarm.
mechanism: Apple's Vision framework reads the elbow angle from each camera frame, and a One Euro filter smooths out the jitter. A small state machine counts a rep only after a full up, down, up cycle, with each phase held for two frames. Reading joints at very low confidence made counting worse, not more forgiving: Vision starts guessing where hidden joints are, and a wrong angle can reset the cycle while a missing one only pauses it.

Vision body-pose request on each front-camera frame
One Euro filter; visible arms weighted by confidence
Up, down, up cycle; 2 frames per phase, 0.18 s minimum phase
Only when every mission is done; a 60 s hold is the logged escape

name: Recruiting OS
line: Tracks 447 recruiting programs and their deadlines, keeps my CRM and drafts outreach into my Drafts folder.
summary: Recruiting OS is a web app on my Mac that tracks 447 finance and quant recruiting programs, most of them summer internships, and marks whether I'm eligible for each. Every deadline carries its source and a confidence label, and deadlines and prep blocks sync to five Google calendars. It also keeps a CRM of people at those firms and writes personalized outreach drafts into my Gmail or Outlook Drafts folder.
why: Job trackers know postings and CRMs know contacts, but none links a contact to the application window at that person's firm. I wanted one place that shows what closes next and who I can write to there.
mechanism: Every claim about me in a draft has to point to evidence in my vault notes. A planner picks only those claims, a writer turns them into a short email, and a verifier holds any draft that fails its checks for grounding, repetition or length, with the reason named. Each deadline keeps its source and a label: official, estimated or secondary.

name: Second Brain
line: The Obsidian vault my agents read before working and write back to after, so every project shares one memory.
summary: My Obsidian vault is the nervous system for everything I build. Claude, Codex and Antigravity each boot from the same five files, find what they need through one index and its wikilinks, and log what they changed in that day's note. Scheduled jobs write into it too: a git snapshot every five minutes, a health audit at 05:00, and on Sundays a fresh chart of the vault followed by a repair pass. The Secretary and the file organizer read it and commit their results back, and the watchdog checks its pulse every hour, so each project works from what the others already know.
why: AI agents forget everything between sessions, and three of them on one Mac will collide or work from stale context. I wanted one memory that every agent loads before it starts and writes to when it finishes.
mechanism: The agents coordinate through the vault rather than through messages, the way ants coordinate through trails. Before a multi-file edit an agent writes a line under In-flight in the day's note, then moves it to its own change log when it finishes, and the next agent reads that before touching anything. A 566-line audit checks links, orphans and frontmatter every morning with a real YAML parser, and the Sunday repair agent fixes what it found and re-runs the audit to confirm each fix.

name: Agent operating layer
line: Skills I wrote that split a prompt into tested units and send each to the right skill.

keyFigure.label: my prompts call a skill I wrote

summary: These are the skills I wrote to sit between my prompt and everything installed on my machine. orchestrate splits a request into work units, gives each unit a test and the one skill built for it from a routing table of 148 skills and commands, and calls a unit done only when its test passes. When nothing installed fits, pathfind searches for an existing tool before anything gets built from scratch, and axe-edge is the research rule underneath both.
why: With that many skills installed, the usual failure is an agent doing the work from memory while the right skill sits unused. The second failure is calling a task done because a tool ran, when no check passed.
mechanism: Every unit of work needs one deliverable and one test it can fail; if the agent can't state the test, it splits the unit again. Routing tries a 15-skill core list, then one of 7 catalogs, then pathfind, and the agent has to say out loud when nothing fits. pathfind makes each probe report what it searched and found nothing for, because a search that lists only hits looks the same as a search that never looked.

One skill per unit: core list, then 7 catalogs, then pathfind

name: Secretary
line: Reads my four inboxes four times a day and turns what needs action into one list and calendar holds.
summary: Four times a day, the Secretary reads my Gmail, university Outlook, iMessage and WhatsApp. Anything that needs action becomes a row in one prioritized Google Sheet and, if it has a date, a tentative 'Maybe:' event on my Google Calendar. Each run starts by reading the brain for context and ends by recording anything durable back in the vault.
why: Deadlines and requests reach me through four apps, and some slipped through. I wanted one ranked list and a calendar that already holds the time.
mechanism: In my Messages database the plain-text field was empty for about 99% of texts, because the words sit in an encoded blob. A 413-line Python reader decodes that blob straight from the local database, which took recovery from 1 of 200 messages to 199 of 200. Every item lands in one of four priority tiers and is matched against existing rows and events on a stable key, so a request that shows up in two apps becomes one row and one hold.

name: ZETA
line: Times every question of the Zetamac mental-math drill and picks what I practice next.
summary: ZETA is a Chrome extension and a dashboard for Zetamac, the 120-second arithmetic drill used in trading-interview prep. The extension records how long I take on every problem, and the dashboard decides what I should drill next. As of the v189 build on 2 October it held 328 runs and 15,293 timed questions.
why: Zetamac only reports a final score, which doesn't say why a run was slow. I wanted to see which problem types cost me time, and to change my practice only when the evidence was strong.
mechanism: The extension watches the problem text and the answer box, timestamps each keystroke, and files every problem under one of 26 families such as x12 or division by 8. A family counts as weak only after 15 observations across 2 runs show it at least 1.2 times slower than its operation's median. Training focus changes only at a scheduled review after three mixed runs, so one noisy run can't redirect practice.

name: Job Watchdog
line: An hourly check that every scheduled job on my Mac made the thing it was supposed to make.
summary: Every hour, a Ruby script checks each scheduled job on my Mac by looking for the thing that job was supposed to make: a dated note, a commit, a log line, a fresh timestamp. Problems arrive as a macOS notification and as one line at the top of each new Claude session. A separate hook runs a real YAML parser over the frontmatter of every note Claude writes to the vault.
why: A scheduled job can finish, produce nothing, and leave only a log line nobody reads. I wanted to hear about it the same day.
mechanism: The rule is to check the output, never the exit code. A check names an artifact and how old it may get, using one of 10 check types; if the script can't read the artifact, the job is marked NOT CHECKED rather than ok, and a paused job that starts running again goes to the top of the list. The watcher also watches itself: if it crashes or fails to rewrite its status file within 120 seconds, a wrapper sends its own alert.

name: AXE_OS
line: Rules for my agents written as checked CUE code, each paired with a note explaining why.
summary: AXE_OS turns one habit into rules my agents follow: before building anything non-trivial, look for what already exists. The rules that can be checked live in 13 CUE files, a typed configuration language, and the reasons behind them live in 39 linked Markdown notes. For ordinary non-trivial work my agents load a compact edition called EDGE, a single 7,340-byte instruction file, and the full system comes in for the hardest builds.
why: Agents start coding with whatever they already know and retry a failing command the same way again. Prompt files drift, too: a project note can quietly contradict a global rule, and nothing notices.
mechanism: Each rule exists twice: as a CUE constraint a validator can check, and as a Markdown note that explains it. A script fails if the code cites a policy note that does not exist, or if a note exists that no code cites. Because CUE merges constraints instead of letting the last file win, a project override can narrow a global rule but can never loosen it.

name: Finder Organizer
line: An AI proposes where each loose file goes; a script decides, logs it, and can undo it.
summary: Every Sunday, a job tidies my Downloads and Desktop folders. An AI model reads each loose file's name, a short preview and where it was downloaded from, then proposes a folder. A separate Python script checks that proposal, logs the move, makes it, and can reverse a whole run.
why: Loose files pile up faster than I file them, and many of my scripts expect their files at fixed paths.
mechanism: The model only proposes, as JSON in a fixed schema, and the script applies its own checks whatever the model said. A file moves only if it is unchanged since the scan, old enough, not referenced by another script or note, headed for a known folder, and proposed with at least 0.75 confidence (0.90 for school, career and project folders). Each move is written to a log before it happens, so undo can replay the log backwards.

name: Carta del Cervello
line: My vault drawn as a medieval sea chart: regions sized by notes, shaded by staleness.
summary: chart-corpus is a skill I made that draws a set of linked notes in the style of a medieval portolan sea chart. Each top-level vault folder becomes a stretch of coast sized by its note count and colored by how long since it was touched, lines across the sea count links between folders, and the most-linked notes are named as ports. Every Sunday at 08:45 a job redraws it into one self-contained HTML file inside the vault. The 4 October chart holds 485 notes and 2,334 links, and 44% of those links cross from one folder into another.
why: A dashboard of counts doesn't show which parts of a knowledge base are going stale or cut off. I wanted an instrument I would actually look at.
mechanism: The hard part was measuring age honestly. File dates were useless because they were all rewritten when the vault moved off iCloud, and frontmatter dates cover only about 85% of notes, so the script reads each note's age from git history and states every staleness figure as a minimum. Links come from Obsidian's own resolved link graph, because searching text for brackets misses aliases and invents links.

name: Table Model
line: Reads every hand as it's dealt, models each opponent and prices every option by expected value.
summary: Table Model is a Chrome extension that reads a PokerNow table hand by hand. It builds a profile of each opponent from the hands they have played, estimates what they are likely holding, and shows the highest-EV action and size on a small placard. A side panel shows the EV of every option. It never clicks or bets for me, and I built it for a home game whose players agreed that tools were allowed.
why: The off-the-shelf poker engines I timed took 45 to 172 seconds per flop spot, far too slow for a live hand, and free tools stop at raw stats. I wanted a fast estimate that adjusts to how specific people play, and a way to test whether its numbers held up on real hands.
mechanism: Each opponent's stats, such as how often they choose to enter a pot, are pulled toward table-wide averages until their own sample is large enough to trust. Their likely hands are set from position and betting line, then narrowed after every action, and each option is scored by its equity against those hands combined with the chance they fold. The newest version learns fold rates from my own hand archive and is graded on hands it did not train on. I looked at those test hands more than once while designing it, so only new sessions are a clean test.

name: Unequal Mobilization
line: Across 3,073 U.S. counties, WWII investment followed prewar industry, not the places that lost the most men.
summary: Unequal Mobilization asks whether the American counties that gave the most men in World War II received the most federal war investment. They did not. Per resident, contract dollars correlate with a county's 1940 manufacturing share at 0.69 and with its fatal burden at −0.03, and war plants and military bases follow the same pattern. The investment that did arrive built different towns: through 1970 a war plant raised county manufacturing employment by 39 log points, while a military base raised total employment by 41 log points and lowered measured homeownership by seven and a half points.
why: Research has mapped where American WWII deaths fell and, separately, what war spending did to local economies. I put both in one county panel to test whether the places that gave the men got the money.
mechanism: Deaths and three kinds of investment sit on one per-resident scale for the same counties, which shows three separate allocations: they overlap with each other at only 0.22 to 0.59, against 0.87 for deaths and population. At 3,073 counties the result is tight enough to rule out any link to wartime loss above 0.09 in either direction, and matched comparisons follow plant and base counties to 1970. A 35-stage Python pipeline writes the results tables and maps, and its last stage checks the paper's numbers against those outputs: 362 checks, 0 mismatches.

name: Shopping Together or Searching Separately?
line: Do shoppers buy more when they browse a thrift store with a friend than when they search apart? A pair-level field-experiment design.

keyFigure.label: conditions: browse together, or search apart

summary: This manuscript asks whether shopping with someone changes what you buy. People who shop together differ from people who shop alone, so comparing them mixes up the companion with whatever brought them in together. The design randomizes instead: adult pairs who arrive at a thrift store together are assigned, within each store, date and time block, either to browse together as they planned or to search separately until they meet again at the exit. The outcome is whether each shopper buys anything. This page describes the question and design only. The manuscript is a draft, and its reported estimates are not presented here as findings because the data behind them have not been verified.
why: Thrift stores make the question sharp. Most items are one of a kind, fit and condition are hard to judge, and putting something back can mean losing it, so many choices are neither a clear buy nor a clear pass. If a second opinion changes behavior anywhere, it should be there.
mechanism: Each shopper's purchase is checked against the receipt first, then a bag inspection or a closely matched self-report. The main model compares the two assigned conditions with block fixed effects and pair-clustered standard errors, and is checked with randomization inference. A secondary estimate adjusts for how closely pairs followed their assignment. Three families of intermediate outcomes, validation and confidence, search productivity and breadth, and coordination cost, are named in advance to help read the purchase result, not to split it into causes. The design compares two bundled conditions among natural companions and makes no claim about welfare.

name: Love Island Dynamics
line: Love Island couples modeled as coupled differential equations, with the public vote built in.
summary: Romantic Dynamics Under Public Selection is a 14-page paper that models each Love Island couple as a pair of coupled differential equations and writes the audience vote into the same system. The two combine into a winner index. It ranks the finalist couples by public support on day 53 plus their mutual affection near the finale. Since late July 2025 I have traded Love Island winner markets on Kalshi on my own calls, using the model's reasoning, and earned about $4,000.
why: The show removes jobs, money and logistics, which leaves something close to a lab for dating under a public vote. I wanted to know why some couples settle and others fall apart, and how the audience decides who stays.
mechanism: Each couple is two equations: how fast each person's feelings fade on their own, how strongly each responds to the other, and a term that lets affection feed on itself. With that term off, a couple settles when fading outweighs responding; once it is strong enough, the steady state turns unstable and small swings grow instead of dying out. A separate public-support function scores what voters can see, such as time in the villa and how long a couple has lasted, across three stages of a 53-day season.

Jacobian trace and determinant show when a couple settles
A damped oscillator adds early swings that fade over the season
A support function over five visible covariates, in three stages
Day-53 support plus late mutual affection and noise; top index wins

name: Hand Compass
line: A Hold'em drill table that grades my decisions against solved strategy and labels where each grade comes from.
summary: Hand Compass is a poker trainer. It deals a spot or a full hand for 4 to 8 players, hides the answer until I commit, then grades my choice from Best Move to Blunder with the pot-odds math and a short lesson. When the open-source postflop-solver covers the spot, the grade comes from its solved strategy; everywhere else the result is labeled HEURISTIC, so solved answers and rules of thumb never look alike. The copy on this site runs without the solver, so its grades are labeled HEURISTIC or EXACT MATH.
why: Many poker trainers present rules of thumb as if they were solved strategy. I wanted a drill where every legal action comes from a rules engine, and where solved output, exact math and heuristics are labeled differently.
mechanism: A TypeScript rules engine generates every legal action and settles side pots and split pots with exact chip accounting. A small Rust service on my machine wraps b-inary's postflop-solver and returns a strategy only once a perfect counter-strategy would gain less than 0.5% of the pot against it. Solves are cached against the exact request, so a restart serves them again without recomputing, and preflop, multiway or oversized spots go to a labeled heuristic instead of an invented number.

name: Odyssey: A Living Reckoning
line: A turning wheel for reading Homer's Odyssey, built to sit beside the print text.
summary: Odyssey: A Living Reckoning is a reading instrument for Homer's poem, built on the four-ring wheel I first made for Ovid. Turning the wheel opens a reading sheet for any of the 185 episodes. Other workspaces hold the forty-day count, descent charts for 17 houses, records for 297 figures and a 118-entry lexicon. Reading progress and margin notes save in the browser and export as JSON.
why: The Odyssey tells its story out of order: about forty days of present action hold ten years of wandering, told in one night by the only witness. Read book by book, it is easy to lose track of who someone is and whose account you are hearing.
mechanism: One file, SPINE.json, lists the 24 books and 185 episode titles, every other data file uses those titles as keys, and a check script flags any title that drifts or any cast name with no figure record. Ovid organizes his poem by transformation and Homer by return, so the slot that named each metamorphosis on the Ovid wheel became the turn: Nobody → Odysseus, Stranger → guest. Each figure gets an engraved seal generated from its name, so the same name always draws the same seal.

name: Metamorphoses: A Living Chronology
line: A four-ring compass for Ovid's 15 books: turn it to any book, then open any of its episodes.
summary: The centerpiece is a compass of four rings: Ovid's six mythic eras, his 15 books, the episodes of the book you are reading and its theme lenses, around an engraved sun inscribed Omnia mutantur, nihil interit. Drag it, scroll it or use the arrow keys, and the inner rings refill with the new book's episodes and themes. Click an episode and its folio slides open beside the wheel with the scene, a numbered account of what happens and a woodcut plate. Around the compass sit descent charts for 15 houses, a transformation network and a sea chart of 141 places, and the Odyssey and Liaozhai instruments copy its design.
why: Ovid runs myth into myth for 15 books, and the cast lists of the 120 episodes use 393 distinct names. A reader needs to see who someone is and what they turn into without leaving the page.
mechanism: Every ring on the compass is computed from the data by one pure geometry module, with curved labels so episode titles read in full and a star band that plots one constellation per book from star coordinates. The descent charts treat family as a graph: a figure's generation is the longest chain of parents above it, and spouses share a row, so Harmonia sits beside Cadmus instead of below him. A test fails if a row mixes generations or a figure is drawn twice.

name: Liaozhai: The Unofficial Register
line: Pu Songling's Strange Tales sorted into 15 reading paths on a concentric dial.
summary: Liaozhai: The Unofficial Register is a reading instrument for Pu Songling's Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio, read in English translation. It groups 30 representative tales into 15 reading paths on a draggable concentric dial, with a live dossier for each tale, a tale ledger, a relationship graph and a chart of recurring story places. Reading state is tracked per tale, and the whole thing ships as a single HTML file that opens offline.
why: The collection has hundreds of tales and no single plot. A reader needs paths through it and quick context on recurring figures, on institutions like the civil-service exam, and on motifs like fox spirits.
mechanism: It carries the Metamorphoses design onto React 19 and TypeScript, with the dial geometry kept in pure functions. The catalog is typed, and a Vitest test asserts exact record counts and that every reading path holds exactly two tales, so a bad data edit fails the test run. The relationship graph and the story chart load only when opened.

name: ChomChom
line: Learning and mindfulness games for young kids. I designed the startup's lesson pipeline.
summary: ChomChom is a startup that makes learning and mindfulness games for young children, built with neurodivergent kids in mind. From April 2024 to May 2025 I was its Product Architect, reporting to the founder. ChomChom Tech was named a 2025 CODiE Awards Finalist in two categories in September 2025.
why: Young kids need lessons matched to their reading level and sensory tolerance, which generic content and unguarded generative AI don't give them. As a student with ADHD, I was building the kind of adaptive learning system I needed when I was younger.
mechanism: The ingestion pipeline I designed enforced one schema on every lesson and scrubbed content for safety. Each lesson was then tagged with reading level, teaching intent and sensory load, so the app could route a child to a suitable next lesson and track progress over time. For the generative-AI mini-games, I added regression tests that catch prompt drift.

name: QVR Advisors
line: A quantitative research internship at a volatility-focused investment firm: ETF rebalancing flows and the implied volatility surface.
summary: QVR Advisors is a volatility-focused investment firm. From June to December 2025 I was a quantitative research intern there, full-time through August and part-time after. My research topic was how mechanical ETF rebalancing can leave short-lived mispricings in options and volatility markets, and how to model the implied volatility surface. This page stays at role level: the code, data and results belong to the employer.
why: Yield-focused and volatility-linked ETFs trade on fixed schedules, and flows that predictable can leave short-lived mispricings in options and VIX futures. The question was whether they can be forecast once the test is honest and out of sample.
mechanism: The work ran on four threads: the options supply that scheduled fund rebalancing creates, real-time fair values for VIX-linked ETFs, the implied volatility surface, and backtests that had to survive cross-validation and significance tests. I implemented and studied standard frameworks such as SVI and Dupire local volatility. What I kept from it is a rule for my own models: a model earns trust when it survives stress, not when it fits the past.

name: Cloudflare (NET) Pitch
role: Led the pitch and built the reverse DCF
line: A reverse DCF of the growth Cloudflare's $191.58 share price already assumed.
summary: A stock pitch on Cloudflare built around a reverse DCF of the growth its $191.58 price already assumed. The thesis was that Cloudflare had become AI infrastructure: it charges for traffic rather than seats, so traffic from AI agents feeds its revenue. Remaining performance obligations up 48 percent and free cash flow up 56 percent to $261 million backed the case for enterprise demand and profitability. Four weighted scenarios gave a target of $242.53 against $191.58, or 26.6 percent upside.
why: Tech stocks had sold off on fears that AI would weaken seat-based software pricing. Cloudflare charges for usage, not seats, so the pitch asked whether the selloff had mispriced it.
mechanism: A reverse DCF runs a valuation backwards: it starts from today's price and solves for the growth the market must already expect. At a 10.8 percent cost of capital and a 30x free-cash-flow exit multiple, $191.58 implied revenue growth of 44 percent a year for 5 years, or 20 percent a year for 10. A customer-level revenue build through 2032 then fed four scenarios, from $70.28 in the bear case to $535.89 in a super-bull case where it charges AI crawlers for access and takes share from hyperscalers.

name: AppFolio (APPF): The Second Act
line: A stock pitch built from nine annual 10-Ks: AppFolio now grows by earning more from each customer.
summary: The Second Act is a 21-slide pitch on AppFolio, a property-management software company. Its thesis is that customer growth is flattening, so the company's second act is earning more from each customer. Revenue per customer rose from $10,520 in 2016 to $38,210 in 2024, value-added services climbed to 76.2 percent of revenue, and GAAP operating margin went from −15.3 percent in 2022 to 17.1 percent in 2024. I pulled the figures from the company's filings, kept the data as small CSVs and charted it in R.
why: AppFolio's customer count was leveling off. I wanted to separate growth from new customers and growth from bigger contracts, to see whether the company still had room to grow.
mechanism: Revenue equals customers times units per customer times revenue per unit, so splitting each year's revenue change into those three pieces shows which one did the work. A logistic curve fitted to customer counts reaches 24,204 by 2030, with each year's gain smaller than the last. Over 2016 to 2024, revenue per customer grew 17.5 percent a year against 9.5 percent for customers.

name: NotebookLM Study Loop
line: Turns finance study material into two audio lessons and a quiz every morning.
summary: Every morning a scheduled job pulls new finance study material that a mentor emails me, adds it to a pinned NotebookLM notebook, and generates two audio lessons and an adaptive quiz. Every Wednesday a second job writes a 90-minute exam. The first pack landed on May 29, 2026, and every daily run since June 11 is logged.
why: I wanted daily interview practice built from the material I was actually being sent, without writing each quiz myself.
mechanism: Making an episode marks a concept as taught, never as mastered. The script estimates my confidence from whether macOS shows I opened each episode file, but caps that estimate at 2 of 3, so only my own rating can mark a concept mastered and retire it from review. I added the cap after an early version made a podcast on LBOs before I had learned LBOs.
